newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico government blasted for role in peace process.
newsitem.headline: Mexico government blasted for role in peace process.

text.p: A congressional peace negotiator on Wednesday blamed hardliners in the Mexican government for the lack of progress in peace talks with armed rebels in the southeastern state of Chiapas.

"We think that hardline sectors in the Mexican state have tolerated and permitted" a breakdown in the peace process, Congressman Jose Narro, a member of the peace commission known as Cocopa, told reporters.
Narro, of the opposition Workers Party, is a former spokesman for Cocopa and one of its most influential members.

Cocopa is attempting to broker a peace deal between the Mexican government and guerrillas of the Zapatista National Liberation Army (EZLN), who launched a brief revolt on Jan. 1, 1994 in which about 145 people were killed.
Peace negotiations are at an impasse with no outward signs that they are about to get back on track.

Cocopa mediated an agreement on Indian rights between the government and the Zapatistas a year ago, a deal that was to be a precursor to a more difficult pact on political and judicial reform. But the Zapatistas stormed out of the talks late last year when the two sides disagreed on the wording of draft legislation on the issue.
For now, the EZLN rebels are holed up in the jungles of Chiapas, surrounded by the Mexican army as a precarious ceasefire holds.

Narro said Zapatista tactics were complicating the peace process, but, "We think that the government side above all has been acting in a way that leads to greater violence and uncertainty in the peace process."
Shooting between the Zapatistas and government troops only lasted for two weeks in 1994, but there has been an uneasy peace since.
